common_name: Canada Red Rhubarb (Cold-Hardy Sweet Red Rhubarb)

planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant; Canada Red performs best in zones with reliable cold winters that provide the extended chilling rhubarb needs for vigorous dormancy break and growth, and it is milder and sweeter than many green-stalked rhubarb varieties.

directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Canada Red is a cold-hardy rhubarb cultivar prized for its uniformly deep red stalks that stay red all the way through the flesh, not just the skin, along with a sweeter, milder flavor than many tart green-stalked rhubarb varieties, meaning less sugar is needed when cooking. It performs best in climates with cold winters that satisfy its chilling requirement for strong spring growth, making it less reliable in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, and always discard the leaves, which are toxic and should never be eaten.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; Violetta requires vernalization, a period of cool temperatures around 50 degrees F for about 10 days, once seedlings have several true leaves, to trigger flower bud formation in the first year.

directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after vernalization. Violetta is a classic Italian heirloom artichoke producing smaller, tender, purple-tinged buds traditionally harvested young and eaten whole, including the tender inner leaves and heart, either braised, fried, or grilled in traditional Italian preparations like carciofi alla romana. The striking violet-purple coloring on the bud scales, especially pronounced in cooler weather, makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Like other seed-grown artichokes it can flower and produce a harvest the first year if properly vernalized as a young seedling, and in mild-winter zones it may persist as a short-lived perennial for a second season of harvest.

common_name: Jersey Giant Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Hybrid Asparagus)

planting.note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Giant is an all-male hybrid that puts no energy into seed production, channeling more resources into thick, vigorous spear growth and higher yields than older open-pollinated varieties.

directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge over the growing season. Jersey Giant is one of the Rutgers University all-male hybrid asparagus cultivars, bred so that plants never set seed and instead direct all their energy into producing thick, vigorous, high-yielding spears over a long productive lifespan. It also carries good resistance to Fusarium crown and root rot, a serious disease problem in older asparagus plantings, making it one of the more reliable modern choices for a home asparagus bed. Do not harvest any spears the first year and only lightly the second year, allowing the fern-like foliage to grow through summer to build a strong root system for many years of future harvests.

common_name: Jersey Supreme Asparagus (Early High-Yield Rutgers Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Supreme is an improved Rutgers all-male hybrid selected for earlier spring emergence and higher total yield than older asparagus cultivars.

directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. Jersey Supreme is a later-generation Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus bred for earlier spring spear emergence and higher overall yield than older selections like Jersey Giant, while retaining the same good disease resistance and long-term productivity that made the Jersey series a standard choice for home and commercial asparagus plantings. As an all-male hybrid it never sets seed, so all of the plant's energy goes into vigorous spear production over what can be a fifteen-to-twenty-year productive bed lifespan. Avoid harvesting the first year and harvest only lightly the second year to let the root system establish fully before full production begins.

common_name: UC 157 Asparagus (Classic California Commercial Hybrid Asparagus)

planting.note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; UC 157 is a classic hybrid asparagus bred at the University of California, valued for concentrated, uniform spear emergence that suits both machine and hand harvesting.

directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. UC 157 is a long-standing, widely planted hybrid asparagus developed by the University of California, prized for producing spears in a more concentrated, uniform flush than many older varieties, along with good heat tolerance that suits warmer growing regions better than some Northeastern-bred cultivars. It has been a mainstay of commercial asparagus production for decades and performs well in home gardens too, given deep, well-drained soil and full sun. As with other asparagus, avoid harvesting the first year and harvest lightly the second year to let the crown establish a strong root system for many years of future spring harvests.
